clue.text: Nerves? Lie and relax, briefly

parts.note: a fib is a small lie

indicators.note: cut short, so the last letter of the word for relax is dropped

parts.note: to rest is to relax

explanation.surface: Advice to someone anxious: lie down and unwind for a little while.
explanation.walkthrough: REST loses its final T to 'briefly'. The question mark marks nerves as an example of fibres.
explanation.definitionFit: Nerves are bundles of fibres in the body, so they are one kind of the thing defined, as the question mark admits.

clue.text: 'Opes 'is 'at, regularly lost, is over 'ere!

indicators.note: every other letter is dropped at a regular interval, keeping the second, fourth and so on

parts.note: the dropped-aitch phrase whose alternate letters are kept

explanation.surface: A Cockney voice: he hopes his hat, regularly mislaid, has turned up over here.
explanation.walkthrough: From OPESISAT, losing O, E, I and A leaves the call. The dropped aitches set a Cockney tone that suits the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A whispered hiss used to catch someone's attention, much like calling 'over here!' quietly.

clue.text: Perhaps roses for Yuppies

definitions.meaning: first meaning: plants that grow up walls or trellises, of which some roses are examples
second meaning: social ..., ambitious young professionals pushing up the social ladder

explanation.walkthrough: Climbing roses are a familiar garden type; yuppies were the 1980s byword for social climbing.
explanation.definitionFit: Rambling roses grow upward on supports, and ambitious young professionals strive upward socially; both are ascenders of a kind.

clue.text: Four Across done first of all? Fancy!

indicators.note: the opening letter of each of the three words is taken

parts.note: first letter of Four
first letter of Across
first letter of done

explanation.surface: A solver delighted at finishing this very clue before any other.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is itself 4 Across, which makes the surface self-referential.
explanation.definitionFit: A passing craze or whim is a fancy, a short-lived enthusiasm.

clue.text: Writer experienced US jail

parts.note: to have felt something is to have experienced it
pen is American slang for a penitentiary, a prison

explanation.surface: An author who has done time in an American prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' suggests a novelist, but it is the pen itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen with a fibre tip is an instrument used for writing, so it is a writer in the tool sense.

clue.text: Terpsichorean cared about entertaining knight

indicators.note: holding a guest inside, so one piece goes within the other
shows the letters of cared are moved around into a new order

parts.note: the anagram fodder
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A ballerina who looked after a knight she was hosting.
explanation.walkthrough: CARED rearranged as DACER takes N inside. Terpsichore is the Greek Muse of dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Terpsichorean means relating to dancing, and as a noun a performer of dance, after the Muse Terpsichore.

clue.text: Roundabout in Petersham bad for air?

indicators.note: places the ring-shaped letter within the jumbled place name
the letters of the place name go wrong and get rearranged

parts.note: the anagram fodder, a district near Richmond in London
a roundabout is circular, like the letter O

explanation.surface: Asking whether a traffic roundabout in Petersham, a part of south-west London, is polluting the air.
explanation.walkthrough: PETERSHAM rearranged gives ATMSPHERE, and the O goes in after the M.
explanation.definitionFit: The envelope of gases around the Earth is the air we breathe; the question mark flags the loose synonym.

clue.text: Protective wear over trousers for those holding post

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece sits above the other

parts.note: chain mail is armour worn for protection
bags is an old British word for loose trousers, as in Oxford bags

explanation.surface: Armour worn over the trousers by those holding a military post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Post' looks like a position held; it is letters and parcels.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacks used by the postal service carry letters and parcels, so they hold mail.

clue.text: Evil pals concocted something to ward off the chaps

definitions.text: something to ward off the chaps

indicators.note: something concocted is mixed up, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Wicked friends brewing up a potion to keep the men away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chaps' reads as men, but it means chapped skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A balm for the mouth protects against chapping, the cracked dryness of cold weather.

clue.text: Halt manuscript's extract for film director

indicators.note: an excerpt lifted from inside the words that follow

parts.note: the run of letters that holds the name

explanation.surface: An order to stop a script's excerpt from reaching a movie maker.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Altman directed M*A*S*H and Nashville.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Altman was an American who made feature movies such as Nashville and Gosford Park.

clue.text: Crime that I cracked? It's not all adding up

indicators.note: broken apart, so the letters fall into a new order

parts.note: the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A detective puzzling over a crime they solved that still does not add up.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: sums involve subtracting, multiplying and dividing as well as adding.
explanation.definitionFit: Elementary calculation covers subtraction, multiplication and division too, so it is more than addition.

clue.text: Son beginning to like wearing glasses in capital

indicators.note: the glasses are put on around the other letters

parts.note: a pair of spectacles looks like two round lenses, OO

indicators.note: takes just the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: first letter of like

explanation.surface: A son who is starting to enjoy wearing his glasses in the city.
explanation.walkthrough: OO as a picture of spectacles is a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Oslo is the chief city and seat of government of Norway.

clue.text: Property in spacious car

definitions.meaning: first meaning: land and buildings someone owns
second meaning: an ... car, a British term for a station wagon

explanation.surface: Someone's belongings stashed inside a roomy vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: An estate car is the British name for a station wagon.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a landed holding and a long-backed car with a large luggage area.

clue.text: Friend saving fine Rhode Island ruin

indicators.note: in the sense of except, so these letters are left out

parts.note: the word letters are taken from
F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencil leads
RI is the US state abbreviation for Rhode Island

explanation.surface: A friend rescuing someone from a fine that would ruin them in Rhode Island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saving' looks like rescuing, but it means 'except': FRIEND without F and RI.
explanation.definitionFit: To destroy something is to put an end to it, so the verb works as ruin.

clue.text: Great hotel breaks, everything included

indicators.note: the words are broken up and reassembled in another order

parts.note: the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An advert for all-inclusive holiday breaks at a grand hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaks' reads as holidays but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means in total, with all counted, which is what an inclusive package offers.

clue.text: One pauper leaving Portugal, possibly Spanish?

indicators.note: the named letter goes out of the jumbled pool
suggests the letters could be arranged otherwise

parts.note: the anagram fodder
P is the international vehicle code for Portugal

explanation.surface: A poor man leaving Portugal who might be Spanish.
explanation.walkthrough: ONE PAUPER minus P leaves ONEAUPER, which rearranges. The question mark says Spanish is just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spaniard belongs to a nation of the continent, so Spanish is one example of the broader word.

clue.text: Maybe Susie is close to vet, one treating canine?

parts.note: Susie Dent is the lexicographer of the UK TV word show Countdown; 'Maybe' marks her as an example of a Dent

indicators.note: the end letter of the word that follows

parts.note: last letter of vet

explanation.surface: Wondering whether Susie is nearly a vet, someone who treats dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canine' looks like a dog, which suits 'vet', but it is the pointed tooth.
explanation.definitionFit: A canine is a pointed tooth, and the person who treats teeth is a tooth doctor.

clue.text: Checked cotton fabric cut up

indicators.note: in a down entry, the letters are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: denim is a twilled cotton cloth
to axe is to cut

explanation.surface: A checked shirt of cotton cut into pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: DENIMAXE written upwards gives the answer. 'Checked' looks like a pattern but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To have inspected something carefully is to have looked it over, a past-tense synonym.

clue.text: Transpose final couplet in Shakespeare sonnet?

indicators.note: the closing pair of letters of the next word

parts.note: its last two letters are taken
a sonnet is a form of verse

explanation.surface: A suggestion to swap the closing two lines of a Shakespeare sonnet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Final couplet' looks like the two closing lines of a sonnet, but it means the last two letters of Shakespeare, RE.
explanation.definitionFit: To swap the order of things is to turn them back to front, a verb synonym.

clue.text: With no introduction, pop medley awkwardly taken on

indicators.note: clumsily arranged, so the letters are mixed
the opening letter of the next word is dropped

parts.note: loses its first letter
part of the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A pop medley performed clumsily, with no proper opening.
explanation.walkthrough: POP without its first letter gives OP, which joins MEDLEY to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone hired has been given a job, the same as taken on by an employer.

clue.text: Raised first of readings on sin

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifted letters are read from bottom to top
takes the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: first letter of readings
re means on or about, as in business letters

explanation.surface: A preacher raising the opening lessons on the topic of sin.
explanation.walkthrough: R plus RE gives RRE, which written upwards becomes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To do wrong is to go astray morally, and the verb is a direct synonym for transgress.

clue.text: Watch Sky for this item that follows the news

definitions.text: Watch Sky for this item that follows the news

parts.words: Watch Sky for this item that follows the news
parts.note: looking up at the sky tells you what conditions are coming, and the forecast is the TV segment straight after the bulletin

explanation.walkthrough: Sky is also a British TV broadcaster, so 'Watch Sky' reads as viewing a channel and as looking upward.
explanation.definitionFit: The forecast slot follows the TV news bulletin, and skies show rain or shine conditions.

clue.text: Speech in late summer kept back by actress Jessica

indicators.note: held within, so one part sits inside the other

parts.note: Jessica Lange is an American film actress

indicators.note: the letters are turned round to read backwards

parts.note: AUG is the abbreviation for August, a month late in the summer

explanation.surface: A speech delivered in late summer that the actress held back.
explanation.walkthrough: Jessica Lange won Oscars for Tootsie and Blue Sky; 'kept back' splits into two signals, 'kept' for containment and 'back' for reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: Spoken or written words as a system of communication are a tongue, and speech is a sense of it.

clue.text: Calm ostrich? Not quite … not quite

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is used, a stretch tucked within it

parts.note: the words containing the answer

explanation.surface: A placid ostrich that is not entirely calm.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated phrase does two jobs: the first signals that only part of the words is used, the second is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means nearly but not entirely, exactly what the second phrase says.

clue.text: Eye police officer quietly ejecting student

indicators.note: throwing one letter out so another takes its place

parts.note: peeler is an old British name for a policeman, after Sir Robert Peel
L is for learner, as on a learner driver's plate
P is piano, the musical direction to play quietly

explanation.surface: A policeman quietly throwing a student out of somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: In PEELER, P replaces the L.
explanation.definitionFit: Peeper is informal slang for an eye, something you look out of.

clue.text: Less demanding because I learn periodically

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every second letter is picked

parts.note: the letters it is picked from

explanation.surface: Finding things less hard because one learns now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters of BECAUSEILEARN are used.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of a word meaning simple or effortless matches less demanding.

clue.text: Was too late in the auditorium for film

indicators.note: an auditorium is where an audience listens, so what is heard counts

parts.note: if you missed something you were too late for it

explanation.surface: Arriving too late at the cinema for the movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' looks like a movie, suiting the auditorium, but it is a thin layer.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin layer of condensation, as on a window, is a film of fine droplets.

clue.text: Still lacking proposal at the AGM?

parts.note: at a company's annual general meeting, a proposal put to the vote is a motion
less means without, as in a suffix like penniless

explanation.surface: An AGM still without any proposal on the table.
explanation.walkthrough: The suffix goes at the end even though 'lacking' comes first in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Something completely stationary is not moving at all, which is the adjective sense of still.

clue.text: Boor not here to support Liberal

indicators.note: in a down entry, the supporting part sits below the other

parts.note: someone out is away, not here

explanation.surface: An uncouth man who is absent rather than backing the Liberals.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry the supporting part goes underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: An oafish, ill-mannered person is a yob or boor, a crude and aggressive type.

clue.text: Noisy Brexiteers in bars

indicators.note: says the word is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: those who voted for Britain to leave the EU were called Leavers

explanation.surface: Loud Brexit supporters holding forth in pubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bars' looks like pubs, a natural home for loud Brexiteers, but it means rigid rods.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigid rods used to prise or lift things are crowbars, so bars in that sense.

clue.text: Former news chief eating sweet, fulfilled

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife

indicators.note: taking something in, so the other piece goes inside

parts.note: ED is short for editor, head of a newspaper
cute means sweet or endearing

explanation.surface: An ex-newspaper boss tucking into a dessert, contented.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' looks like a pudding, but it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A plan that has been carried out has been accomplished, so it is completed or achieved.

clue.text: Rise of Rocky character is nonsense, looking back

indicators.note: the letters face the other way, read from end to start

parts.note: rot is nonsense or rubbish

explanation.surface: Dismissing as rubbish the idea that the boxer Rocky's rise is in character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocky' looks like the boxing film, but means stony.
explanation.definitionFit: A tor is a craggy hill, especially on Dartmoor, an elevation made of rock.
